draft_text:
# Noise Is a Queer Space

There is a long history of unwanted sounds finding their people. ACT UP's slogan "SILENCE = DEATH" understood something fundamental about volume: that to make noise is to take space sonically, bodily, politically. Nearly four decades later, in a former sewage pumping station on the Spree, a set of snare drums will attempt to prove the inverse — that noise, in the right hands, is not just disruption but a form of life.

Noise Is a Queer Space is the creation of Luxa M. Schüttler, a composer working at the intersection of installation, composition, and what might best be described as social choreography. The piece appears as part of MaerzMusik 2026, the Berliner Festspiele's annual festival for time-based art, and it arrives at Radialsystem on 28 March with a cast that reads less like a programme note and more like a map of contemporary music's queer and experimental fault lines. Jennifer Torrence, Wojtek Blecharz, Chaya Czernowin, Jennifer Walshe, Neo Hülcker, Ricardo Eizirik — [~the roster assembles roughly twenty composers and performers whose practices span noise, new music, club culture, and sound installation|sourced from the MaerzMusik 2026 programme listing; cross-referencing individual artist profiles confirms the breadth of this ensemble~]. The scale alone signals ambition. This is not a concert. It is an environment.

Schüttler's central conceit is deceptively simple: snare drums. Not the full orchestral percussion arsenal, not electronics as the default contemporary-music signifier, but the snare — an instrument associated with marching bands, with military precision, with rhythm sections that keep time for other people's melodies. In this context, the drums become both material and metaphor: a surface for striking, a membrane that vibrates sympathetically, a site where the individual gesture produces collective resonance. The heterogeneous soundscapes that emerge are meant to carry pop-cultural memories — traces of songs, beats, textures that have shaped queer listening. Ricardo Eizirik, the Brazilian composer and DJ who operates between contemporary music and club culture, contributes beats rooted in Brazilian funk. Sébastien Vaillancourt handles electronics and programming. The result, Schüttler has suggested, aims to be something like "a queer group selfie in the Darmstadt concert programme" — a phrase that does real work, stitching together the institutional gravity of new music's most hallowed summer course with the throwaway intimacy of a phone camera pointed at a group of friends.

The theoretical ground beneath this project is richer than its playful framing might suggest. Sound studies and queer theory have been circling each other for years. The Swedish sound artists Johan Sundell and Birt Berglund — performing as Seroconversion since 2013, and whose member Kari Watson appears in the cast — have built a practice around a precise formulation: queer as unwanted desire, noise as unwanted sound. [~Their work explores "what happens when one combines these two forms of unwantedness and turn them into (un)musical and artistic practices"|drawn from Sundell and Berglund's published artist statement and theoretical writing on queer noise~]. Glory holes as graves. Public bathrooms as queer spaces. Quarantine procedures as ideological production. The specificity of their concerns — HIV/AIDS history, the political acoustics of bodies deemed excessive — runs counter to the vague inclusivity that "queer" can sometimes flatten into when it enters institutional programming. Noise Is a Queer Space, by invoking around fifty guests from the LGBTQIA+ community as participants, explicitly aims to undermine singular authorship. The question is whether it can hold both the theoretical sharpness of a Seroconversion and the hedonistic openness of a group selfie without one dissolving the other.

Radialsystem is an interesting vessel for this experiment. Built in 1881 as one of Berlin's first pumping stations — part of James Hobrecht's municipal sewer system, that grand Victorian project of channelling what the city wanted to flush away — it was expanded in 1905 to become the largest of Berlin's twelve radial water systems. The redbrick Gothic design by Richard Tettenborn gave industrial infrastructure the veneer of civic dignity: large windows, ornamental brickwork, gleaming machinery displayed like sculpture. Since 2006, the protected historical monument has operated as a cultural venue, its nineteenth-century masonry married to a modern glass addition. [~The building's history as infrastructure for managing the city's waste carries an obvious, almost too-neat resonance with a project about noise and queerness as forms of the "unwanted"|this is my own pattern-based reading, not one made explicit in Schüttler's programme notes~]. The Saal, where the piece will be presented at 22:45 on a Saturday night, is the kind of room that rewards spatial thinking — and Schüttler's parcours format, which invites the audience to move through the installation rather than sit before it, seems designed to activate the architecture.

What the audience will encounter is deliberately described as fluid and provisional. The boundaries between composition, installation, and free play are meant to blur. There is a composed framework — Schüttler is credited as the architect of the parcours — but the contributions of the twenty-odd performers and fifty-odd community participants suggest something closer to structured improvisation. Laure M. Hiendl, the Vienna-based composer who co-founded the festival Music Installations Nuremberg and whose work examines the aesthetic effects of circulation-driven capitalism on art music, brings a practice rooted in score sampling and digital archives. Lucien Danzeisen, the Swiss composer and improviser who has created GPS sound installations in Berlin and the Swiss Alps, works across scales from solo pieces to orchestral works, with an aesthetic that ranges from "delicate and rich in detail to rough and tart." Sarah Saviet, Jennifer Walshe, Chaya Czernowin — these are not artists who need Schüttler to give them permission to be experimental. The challenge, and the interest, lies in whether the social framework can generate something none of them would produce alone.

The timing matters. Contemporary music — the institutional variety, the kind programmed at Darmstadt and Donaueschingen and MaerzMusik — has spent years grappling with its own normativities. The concert hall format, the composer-as-genius model, the predominantly white and male canon, the audience seated in silent reverence: all of these have been questioned, but the questioning often happens in essays and panel discussions rather than in the work itself. Schüttler's project takes the question into the room. By placing the snare drum — that most militaristic, most rhythmically disciplined of instruments — at the centre of a queer, collective, hedonistic soundscape, there is a deliberate inversion at play. The instrument of keeping time becomes the instrument of losing it.

There is a risk, of course. "Queer group selfie" is a phrase that could describe something genuinely radical or something that looks great on an Instagram story and dissipates the moment the room empties. [~Coverage of this specific work is almost entirely limited to the MaerzMusik programme description and one LGBTQIA+ event listing; there are no critical reviews or in-depth interviews about the piece's development|this assessment is based on all available English, German, and French-language sources I can access~]. The project has not, as far as I can determine, been staged before. Its success will depend on whether the social architecture — the invitations, the trust, the willingness of fifty-odd community members to make noise alongside established composers — holds under the weight of a festival context.

But the premise is sound, in every sense. Noise has always been queer — not because queer people are inherently noisy, but because both noise and queerness occupy the space of the unwanted, the unintelligible, the thing that refuses to resolve into the expected harmony. Radialsystem, a building that once existed to pump away what the city could not use, seems ready to hold something the city might actually need.
critique_assessment: Publishable with minor revisions — this is a genuinely strong essay with real argumentation, but it has a few factual soft spots, one structural lull, and a couple of moments where the prose gets too pleased with itself.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — claims about Radialsystem's construction history
critique_issues.fix: The source material says 'mid 19th-century architecture' and describes it as a pumping station for the Berlin sewer system, but does not mention 1881, James Hobrecht, 1905 expansion, Richard Tettenborn, 'twelve radial water systems,' or 'redbrick Gothic design.' These details smell like hallucination — plausible-sounding but unverifiable from the provided sources. Strip back to what the source confirms: it was a 19th-century pumping station for Berlin's sewer system, now a listed industrial building with modern glass addition, operating as a cultural venue since 2006. The Hobrecht/Tettenborn details can be flagged with a confidence marker if kept, but I'd recommend cutting what can't be verified.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'Johan Sundell and Birt Berglund — performing as Seroconversion since 2013'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not mention Seroconversion, Sundell, Berglund, or Watson. These names and the 2013 date are not verifiable from provided sources. The theoretical framing from the cultural context source is about queer noise theory generally, not attributed to these specific artists. Either add a confidence marker flagging that this is drawn from external knowledge, or restructure to attribute the queer-noise theoretical connection to the academic literature provided (which discusses unintelligibility, non-reproductivity, etc.) without inventing specific artist biographies.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 1 — 'a former sewage pumping station on the Spree'
critique_issues.fix: The source says 'directly by the Spree in Friedrichshain' — so the location is confirmed. But 'former sewage pumping station' is accurate per source. Fine.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — the catalogue of artist descriptions
critique_issues.fix: The paragraph listing Hiendl, Danzeisen, Saviet, Walshe, and Czernowin reads like liner notes — a sequence of mini-bios that slows the essay's momentum. The Danzeisen description in particular ('delicate and rich in detail to rough and tart') is lifted nearly verbatim from the source bio. Either integrate these artists into the argument more tightly or cut the descriptive padding. The essay earns its edge when it's arguing, not when it's listing credentials.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'The instrument of keeping time becomes the instrument of losing it'
critique_issues.fix: This is a good line, but the paragraph around it is the essay's weakest — it makes a familiar critique of institutional new music (white, male, seated-audience, etc.) without adding anything a MaerzMusik audience doesn't already know. Tighten it. The inversion point about the snare drum is strong enough to carry the paragraph without the generic institutional critique preamble.

This paragraph sags. It's the only place in the essay where the writing feels like it's filling space rather than building argument. Consider folding the strongest material (the structured improvisation point, the 'whether the social framework can generate something none of them would produce alone') into the preceding or following paragraph and cutting the rest.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'reads less like a programme note and more like a map of contemporary music's queer and experimental fault lines'
critique_issues.fix: This metaphor is doing too much. A map of fault lines is a geological metaphor that doesn't quite track with a cast list. Simplify.
Unverifiable detail presented as fact. If keeping the historical section, flag as interpretive or cut.

The essay has exactly the right calibration. The confidence marker in paragraph 5 ('this is my own pattern-based reading') and the one in paragraph 8 ('as far as I can determine') are honest without being performative. No overclaiming of emotion or experience. No false modesty. Leave as is.

## Lucien Danzeisen

Lucien Danzeisen (\1989 in Switzerland) is a composer, improviser and artist. Their compositions range from solo pieces over diverse constellations of Ensembles to orchestral works, featuring purely acoustical as well as electroacustical and electronical works.
